nameStory: Marsh woundwort gets its name from its wetland habitat and its historical use in treating wounds and injuries. The 'woundwort' part comes from the old belief that this plant could help heal cuts and scrapes when applied directly to the skin. Its scientific name 'palustris' literally means 'of the marsh' in Latin, emphasizing where you're most likely to find this healing herb.
description: Marsh woundwort is a medium-sized perennial herb that grows up to about 3 feet tall in wet areas throughout New England. Like other members of the mint family, it has a square stem and produces spikes of small flowers that attract bees and other pollinators. This European native has naturalized in North America and forms patches in marshy ground with its spreading underground stems. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance but produces attractive purple-pink flower spikes in summer.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The stem is distinctly square when you roll it between your fingers - a classic mint family trait. It feels hollow and somewhat brittle, with a slight roughness to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple-pink flowers are arranged in dense, interrupted whorls around the stem, creating a spiky tower effect. Each tiny flower has the characteristic two-lipped shape of the mint family.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves grow in opposite pairs along the square stem and are lance-shaped with toothed edges. They feel somewhat rough and have a faint, not-quite-minty smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright colonies 2-3 feet tall in wet areas, often creating patches as it spreads by underground stems. The whole plant has a somewhat gangly, informal appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, hard nutlets that develop where the flowers were. These tiny seeds often stick to clothing and fur, helping the plant spread to new wet areas.

habitat: Look for marsh woundwort in wet meadows, along stream banks, pond edges, and in marshy areas with rich, moist soil. It thrives in spots that stay consistently damp but aren't permanently flooded. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants in both sunny and partially shaded wetlands.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground stems in late spring, showing the characteristic square stems and opposite leaves. Young plants are bright green and relatively small at first.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer when the purple-pink flower spikes are most prominent and attractive to pollinators. This is the best time for identification when all features are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into small seed clusters while leaves may turn yellowish. The square stems remain sturdy and identifiable even as the plant begins to die back.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only dried stems that may persist into early winter. The plant survives underground and will re-emerge in spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'woundwort,' this plant is actually edible and the underground tubers were once considered a delicacy - some people say they taste like a cross between artichoke and radish when cooked!
confusionNotes: Marsh woundwort can be confused with other tall wetland mints, but the square stem and marsh habitat are key distinguishing features. Remember: 'Square stem in the swamp' - if you feel that distinctive four-sided stem in wet ground, you've likely found your woundwort.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'woundwort' worry you - while historically used medicinally, this plant is actually quite harmless and even edible. It's completely unrelated to other plants that might sound concerning, and the 'wort' simply means 'plant' in old English.
compareHints: Marsh woundwort differs from its hedge-nettle cousins by its preference for consistently wet habitats rather than just moist woodland edges. Unlike the fuzzy-leaved woolly hedge-nettle that's popular in gardens, marsh woundwort has rougher, less hairy leaves and grows wild in wetlands. Its flower spikes are also more interrupted and less dense than those of most other hedge-nettles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hedge-nettle relatives, this species stands out for its narrow, hyssop-like leaves and preference for wetter habitats.
Unlike other hedgenettles in New England, woolly hedgenettle is the only one with thick, densely woolly leaves that feel soft to touch.
Among New England's hedge nettles, marsh hedge nettle stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, soft-textured leaves and stems compared to its smoother relatives.
Prairie woundwort differs from marsh woundwort by preferring dry rather than wet habitats and having broader, more heart-shaped leaves.
